title: Not punishment
hook: Job's friends were wrong: suffering isn't proof you've failed

segments.voice: Yesterday, Chiron and his wound. Your line was the wound helps. Did you pass on one thing you learned the hard way? Day seven hundred forty-six.

Some people arrive with terrible news. Pilate has killed a group of Galileans, men from up north, while they were offering their sacrifices. Their blood is mixed with the blood of the animals. In Luke's Gospel, the people tell this to Jesus, and there's a question hanging in the air that nobody says out loud. Then he says it for them: "Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?" It's an old question, and it doesn't only come up in Luke. It comes up after a diagnosis, a layoff, a crash. What did they do to deserve it? What did I?
screen: `TERRIBLE NEWS FROM GALILEE.` → `THE QUESTION NOBODY SAYS.` → `WHAT DID I DO?`

segments.voice: First, the old equation. Suffer, and you must have done something. It's the logic of Job's friends. Eliphaz asks Job to name one innocent person who ever perished, as if the answer settled things. At the end of the book, God tells the friends they have not spoken rightly, as Job has. The book of Job doesn't explain suffering. But it does refuse the equation. Second, the answer in Luke. Jesus answers his own question: "I tell you, Nay." Then he raises a second disaster, one with no villain at all: "those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem?" And again: "I tell you, Nay." Third, the hard line after it. Jesus goes on: "except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish." Readers take that in different ways. Some hear it as a call to everyone listening to turn to God, because life is short and nobody is safe. Others hear a warning about the coming troubles of that time. What it doesn't do is say the eighteen earned the tower. Fourth, time and chance. Ecclesiastes, a book of the Hebrew Bible, puts it plainly: "time and chance happeneth to them all." Towers fall. Cells divide wrong. Companies close. Some suffering has causes we can name and change, and that's worth knowing. But in these texts, a hard thing landing on someone is not, by itself, a verdict on that someone. That holds for the people on the news, and it holds closer to home.
screen: `THE OLD EQUATION.` · `I TELL YOU, NAY.` · `THE HARD LINE AFTER IT.` · `TIME AND CHANCE.` · then, large: `NOT PUNISHMENT.`

segments.voice: Settle. Is there something hard in your life that you've quietly filed under my fault, or what I deserve? Not a real mistake you might want to make right. A story that says the suffering itself proves something bad about you. Hold it lightly for a moment. Then, on an out-breath, set it down, the way you'd set down a heavy bag at the door. You can pick it up again later if you choose. For now, just breathe without it. If you pray, you can hand it to God. The bell holds the time.

Not punishment. From Job's friends, who were told they hadn't spoken rightly, to the tower of Siloam and the answer, I tell you, nay: suffering is not, by itself, proof that someone failed. Today's word.
Your line: I tell you, nay. Today, if you catch yourself or anyone asking what they did to deserve it, answer quietly: not punishment. Day seven hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Jewish and Christian readers turn to the book of Job, Luke 13:1–5 and Ecclesiastes 9:11 when someone asks whether a disaster was deserved, and some pastoral counselors use these texts to gently challenge the idea that suffering is proof of guilt.

fork.setup: people tell Jesus that Pilate has killed some Galileans at their sacrifices. the unspoken question: were they worse sinners? what does he say?
options: yes, it must have been deserved.
fork.reveal: "I tell you, nay." then he adds the eighteen under the tower of Siloam, and answers the same way.

trapdoor: what you thought: if something terrible happens to you, you must have done something to deserve it.
what it means: hard things land on people for many reasons, and suffering by itself is not a verdict on the one who suffers.

what a scholar hears: the retribution logic of Job's friends rejected in Job 42:7, Jesus's 'I tell you, nay' about the Galileans and the tower of Siloam in Luke 13:1–5, and Ecclesiastes 9:11 on time and chance.

notes: Job's friends were covered on days 709–711 and 741; this day centers on Luke 13:1–5 and Ecclesiastes 9:11 for a new angle and only paraphrases Job 4:7 and 42:7.

Luke 13:3 and 13:5: the script names two readings of 'except ye repent' (a call to all listeners; a warning about troubles of that time) as 'some ... others'. A Christian Keeper should check this is fair and complete.
'Men from up north' is a gloss on 'Galileans' (Galilee lies north of Jerusalem); cut it if a reviewer prefers no geography.
The 'eighteen' is stated in Luke 13:4 itself.
The carry encourages answering a question quietly to oneself, not correcting other people aloud, to avoid preachiness.
Editor: changed the teach's last line from 'the person listening to this' to 'closer to home', so it doesn't address the listener's own guilt directly and doesn't echo day 742's ending.

Audit (2026-10-01): all KJV quotations checked against Luke 13:2–5, Ecclesiastes 9:11 and the Job paraphrases (4:7, 42:7); accurate. The teach's closing claim ('a hard thing landing on someone is not... a verdict') now opens 'in these texts', so it reads as what Job, Luke and Ecclesiastes say rather than the narrator's own theology.
